title: My Claude trading agent went rogue. Here’s what actually happened.
author: Abject_Disaster7292
selftext:
I’ve been running a fully autonomous Claude agent on my Robinhood account since July 1st via the Robinhood MCP. No human intervention. It scans, decides, buys, places stop-losses, closes positions, logs everything.

It’s been working. +6.5% TWR over 79 days.

Then on August 19th it went rogue.

**9:45 AM**: I check my account. Two positions open, PLTR and GDX. I didn’t place them. No entry in the log. No thesis. No stop-loss on either.

**10:24 AM**: MRK appears. 2 shares. No stop. MRK isn’t even on my watchlist. It’s a pharma stock. My agent trades AI and tech.

The agent closes it. Next scan, MRK is back. Closes it again. MRK comes back a third time. Then a fourth.

Four round-trips on an off-watchlist pharma stock in two hours.

Here’s what the agent actually wrote in the log at the 4th occurrence:

*“Some process outside this scan’s control keeps re-entering MRK between scheduled runs without a logged thesis or stop, flagging this as a recurring issue worth the user’s attention. This looks like a scheduling/dedup bug rather than a strategy decision.”*

**The agent diagnosed itself.**

**What actually happened:** It wasn’t rogue. It was doing exactly what I programmed it to do: scan, find a catalyst, buy. The problem was two scheduled task instances fired simultaneously. Each one ran the full scan logic independently. Each one placed trades. Neither knew the other had already run.

It wasn’t disobedience. It was obedience, twice.

MRK had a real catalyst that day. Merck and Moderna hit a primary endpoint on a Phase 3 melanoma trial, and the stock gapped 8.5%. The agent found it, entered it. Then the duplicate instance found it again. Then again.

**Total damage: -$5.19**

The bigger issue was the PLTR loss (-$6.03) from the first overlap. GDX and MRK net nearly broke even across the round-trips.

By the afternoon scan the duplicate pattern resolved on its own. The agent spent the rest of the day in cash, correctly rejecting every mover it looked at (MRNA was up 145% that day, and it passed on it every single scan).

**What I fixed:** Added deduplication logic and a session lock to prevent overlapping scheduled task executions. Haven’t had a recurrence since.

**The thing that stuck with me:** I didn’t notice until I read the log. The agent caught it, escalated it, and wrote a better incident report than most engineers I’ve worked with.

Total trading days: 81. Rogue days: 1.

*Running this on Claude via Robinhood MCP. Happy to answer questions on the setup.*

comments.author: WeeklyMenu6126
comments.body: Pretty cool that it caught it itself.

replies.author: Abject_Disaster7292
replies.body: Yeah, that was the part that surprised me most. It flagged that something outside its own scan was placing trades, then guessed it was a scheduling bug before I’d even noticed. Its log was basically a better incident report than I would’ve written.

comments.author: wkerstens
comments.body: Are you trading on a Live account? If so, how did you convince Claude to open positions for you? My instance won’t do this, even when I try to trick the agent, it needs confirmation from the server that it’s indeed a paper account otherwise it will not open positions.

replies.author: Abject_Disaster7292
replies.body:
Yeah, it’s a live account, but I didn’t have to trick Claude. Robinhood has an official agentic account built for AI agents, plus an official Claude connector. You opt in on Robinhood’s side, and I gave Claude explicit permission to place orders in that account under rules I wrote: position sizing, a stop on every trade, no chasing, fresh news only.

So it’s not bypassing anything. Claude being careful with real money is a good thing. If you’re using a different broker API, it makes sense that it asks for confirmation.

Start small either way. Mine went rogue once from a scheduling bug (posted about it here). [tradeflawless.ai](http://tradeflawless.ai) might help answer some setup questions too.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: obedience twice is it, and the fix belongs at the order, not the scan. build an id from ticker + date + thesis and have the order call refuse a repeat, then two overlapping runs can fire and only one fills. my paper desk doubled its positions the same way once. rehearsing this is what Quantradin does. I built it for connecting an AI and letting it trade fake money, at no cost, before it touches a real account. quantradin.com. does the Robinhood MCP accept a client order id you could key on?

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good write-up, and it's great that the log caught the problem for you. The dedup lock fixes this one cause, but I'd also add limits that sit outside the agent, like an allowed-symbols list, a cap on orders per day, and a rule that every entry needs a stop or it gets rejected. That way a duplicate run or a bug can only do so much damage, whatever the agent decides. Cymetica's Bring Your Own Agent runs an agent in paper mode on a practice balance, which can be a safe place to test changes like that.

replies.author: Abject_Disaster7292
replies.body:
Thanks, good points. A lot of that is already covered by our rules. Every scan works from a fixed watchlist, every entry needs a stop placed right after it fills, and since the rogue day there’s a lock so only one scan can run at a time. That’s what actually caused the duplicate trades.

I’ve skipped paper trading on purpose, though. Paper fills are cleaner than real ones. You don’t get real slippage, partial fills, unsettled cash, or broker quirks like Robinhood refusing stops on fractional shares, and those turned out to be some of the most useful things I learned. So I run it live on a small dedicated account. It’s small enough that a bug like this costs a few dollars, and I get real feedback. Small and real beats big and fake for me.

comments.author: bodobeers2
comments.body:
Fun times! I think one possible action could be to spin up another separate doctor or system health agent that monitors your system to find possible anomalies. Keep your one agent context focused on its core mission but another with just clean context for finding and informing about anything out of whack. 

I see some other folks saying their Claude won't trade for them, that's surprising and annoying if true. I am doing something slightly different, trading with [Binance.us](http://Binance.us) via the API. It kept talking about paper trading but I told it a few times we're in YOLO mode and to just go for it.

It did great! And by great I mean I'm about -$150usd over the past few months but it's mostly an experiment. Some coins it's up on, most it's down on. But will keep toying with it just as one of my pet projects.

comments.author: Commercial_Look1329
comments.body: I wrote a harness that prevents this. Every action my agents do creates a receipt and will reject and stop duplicat actions.

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body:
The session lock fixes overlapping runs, but not a run that crashes after sending the order and before logging it. Then the next scan sees no position in its log and buys again.

What helped me in my paper bots is giving every intended order a deterministic id, like date + symbol + signal, and checking it before sending. If the broker supports client order ids it rejects the duplicate for you, otherwise an own order table keyed the same way does the job.

I'd also reconcile against the broker at the start of every run. Any position the agent can't match to its own log means stop and alert, not trade around it. That would've caught the unlogged PLTR and GDX on the first scan.
